title: Closed practices
hookLine: some Indigenous and initiatory practices belong to their peoples and aren't ours to borrow

cards: For weeks now, this path has been walking into other people's houses of practice. A Zen hall. A gurdwara.
A Quaker meeting. A Sufi circle. Those doors were open: come and sit, come and eat.
But a few doors in the world are shut on purpose, and a polite visitor learns to notice them. Not shut out of rudeness, and not because the people inside think less of anyone.
Shut because what happens inside belongs to a people, or is given only to those who have been brought in. What does a guest do when one is closed?

teach.h: KEPT FOR MEMBERS OR THE INITIATED.
teach.b: A closed practice is one a community keeps for its own members, or for people it has initiated. In ancient Greece, the rites of Demeter at Eleusis were kept secret by those who took part.

The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, in paraphrase, calls them holy rites that no one may break, pry into, or speak aloud. The hymn happily tells the story of Demeter and her lost daughter. It won't tell you what happened inside.

Story open, rite closed. Today the idea is often raised by some Indigenous peoples. Certain ceremonies, songs and sacred objects belong to a particular nation or family, passed down by those with the right to lead them.
Some Indigenous leaders have asked outsiders, plainly, not to copy their ceremonies or sell versions of them.

Their reasons are theirs to give, and they have given them: these aren't techniques. They're relationships, with a land, with ancestors, with a people's history, including the times those practices were banned or mocked.
Learning about a practice is usually welcome: reading what a community has chosen to share, listening to its own people tell it, attending when you're invited.
Taking it is something else: performing it without the community, borrowing its sacred words for your own use, selling it. And there's a third thing, being invited.
That door opens from the inside, not the outside. A path like this one, drawing from many traditions, has to be honest about where its borrowing stops. Some things are offered.
Some are not mine to take.

how: Communities with closed practices usually share some of their stories and teachings openly while keeping certain ceremonies for members or the initiated; respectful outsiders learn from what the community chooses to share, and take part only when invited by those with the right to lead.

games.q: a weekend workshop online offers to teach you a ceremony from an Indigenous nation, led by someone who isn't from that nation. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: sign up: knowledge should be free.
learn about the ceremony from that nation's own people instead.
try the ceremony at home to see if it works.
games.why: learning about is welcome; taking is something else. some Indigenous leaders have asked outsiders, plainly, not to copy or sell their ceremonies.

practice: Bring to mind a practice that belongs to a particular people, one you've seen copied or been curious about, and don't try it; just hold it with respect, the way you'd stand quietly outside a house where a ceremony is going on.
Ask who has the right to lead it. If you pray, pray for that community; if you don't, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Closed practices. Rites and ceremonies a community keeps for its own members or its initiated, to be learned about with respect and not taken. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: not mine to take. Some doors open from the inside. That's today, done.
